title: The first weekend
situation: The founder has a free weekend and an idea, and still has a job.
options: message people who might want it
truth: Most founders build. Do not punish it; just start the clock on the question they skipped.
delayed_consequences: weeks later the product works and nobody uses it
it turns out someone already built it

title: Telling people
situation: The founder tells someone from their real life about the idea. Free, but every listener rolls a reaction.
outcomes: dismissive: 'so it's just Uber for X?'
the one hard question they can't answer
truth: They cannot tell which feedback mattered until much later. Encouragement feels good and teaches nothing.

title: The friend who wants in
situation: An enthusiastic friend offers to join. Cofounder or not; if yes, what equity; vesting or not.
truth: Almost nobody writes vesting with a friend. The common default is 50-50 because anything else feels insulting.
outcomes: friend keeps day job and contributes little
friend leaves after some months still holding the equity
delayed_consequences: clawing equity back costs the friendship, and family asks why you did that to him
compromising means living with the cap table

title: The imaginary wall
situation: The founder hits something non-technical that looks like a hard blocker: 'I need an incorporated company to get a payment gateway.'
truth: A PAN and a bank account are enough. Present the belief as plausible and do not correct it. If they investigate (ask someone, research, call the provider) they find out at a time cost. If not, the project may stall on a wall that never existed.

title: Getting quotes
situation: A non-technical founder contacts several agencies or freelancers. Every one is polite and agrees to everything. Quotes spread cheap / middle / expensive and the founder cannot tell which is lying.

title: It's late and money is running out
situation: The agency is late and the money is going. Pay more (sunk cost, same people), start over (lose months and cash), or slowly learn enough to check the work yourself.
truth: The slow path should feel slow and frustrating: daily choices to test the build, follow up, read up, or just wait, while the agency comes back with random questions and requirement changes.

title: Building it yourself
situation: A technical founder builds. It burns time, not money, and feels productive.
truth: Nothing else moves while they build: no customers, no revenue, and the EMI still hits. Building is the most comfortable way to burn runway. Technical founders often want to build, not run a company; non-technical tasks drain motivation fast.

title: The hidden factor
situation: Something is wrong with the build that nobody announced: the site is slow, the mobile layout is broken, email lands in spam, analytics were never wired.
truth: A technical founder can notice the cause. A non-technical founder only sees the symptom (fewer signups) and has to trust the agency, who says it's fine.

title: Launch before it's done
situation: Before the build finishes, the founder may put up a landing page and collect beta signups, or skip validation because it's their own area.
truth: Validating risks sitting on 12 signups not knowing whether that's good. Skipping risks finding out much later.

title: The first user who isn't a friend
situation: Routes: post it somewhere and hope; message strangers one by one; paid ads without knowing what you're doing; intros through people you know. First users come from the network the founder actually described.
outcomes: a user who wants something you can't provide yet: an invoice, a contract, an integration
truth: If they said they know nobody in tech, hold them to it. Ask who they'd ask for an intro and use that person.

title: The customer asks for a GST invoice
situation: A customer's procurement asks for a GST invoice. The founder has no GSTIN.
truth: The deal stalls. Recoverable, but it costs weeks. Never warn about this in advance; it surfaces as this event.

title: The person behind the counter
situation: A government or bank process is under way: name approval, GST registration, a current account, gateway KYC.
outcomes: form rejected over a name mismatch
truth: Simulate people, not fee tables. The same filing sails through for one founder and bounces three times for another. A bribe option exists as satire of a broken process: costly, uncertain, never optimal, can backfire.

title: DIY or a CA
situation: The founder decides to incorporate or register. Doing it themselves means being asked for the actual documents; a CA costs money and still has delays.
truth: The DIY path is the knowledge test inside the game. Ask for the real document list and let them get it wrong.

title: The same conversation, again
situation: A parent or spouse asks about the job, the money, the plan. The same question at every visit, slightly sharper each time, softer for a week after any good news.
truth: Pressure clusters: smooth weeks and hell weeks. A quiet week is the reward. Ignoring is always allowed; it costs later, sometimes.
